Since the annealing temperature is above the FCC + L12 dual-phase region [30], the formation of the L12 phase during quenching can be attributed to its rapid precipitation kinetics [53], explaining the high strength of the CRSA alloy.

The inverse pole figure (IPF) image indicated that the CRSA alloy consists of randomly oriented FCC grains without any noticeable texture.
The corresponding grain size distribution, analyzed by Gaussian fitting (Fig. 3c), showed a relatively uniform grain size, with an average of 14.5 ± 4.6 μm.
TEM revealed that the CRSA alloy contained distortion-free recrystallized grains, with only a minimal number of dislocations (Fig. 3d).
The geometry necessary dislocation (GND) density map in Fig. 3b revealed complete recrystallization of the alloy, with an average GND density of 4.1 × 1013/m2.

evidence.section: 3.3.1 Dislocation substructure evolution and microbands development
evidence.quote: During the deformation of FCC alloys containing the ordered L12 precipitates, dislocations cutting through the L12 phase enhanced the ability of subsequent dislocations to traverse the same slip plane, a phenomenon termed “glide plane softening”, thereby improving planar slip [56,57].
